study.citation: Ghimire SK, Gimenez O, Pradel R, McKey D, Aumeeruddy‐Thomas Y (2008) Demographic variation and population viability in a threatened Himalayan medicinal and aromatic herb Nardostachys grandiflora: matrix modelling of harvesting effects in two contrasting habitats. Journal of Applied Ecology 45:41-51. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2664.2007.01375.x
study.notes: Single rhizome harvest (Sept 1998) at 0/10/25/50/75% in outcrop subplots by local amchi; COMPADRE stores 1999-2002 mean matrices. Meadow (244454) is an unharvested population in a different habitat, not a control for outcrop treatments. COMPADRE altitude (4805 m) differs from paper (3800-4200 m): metadata discrepancy logged.

study.citation: GAOUE OG, TICKTIN T (2010) Effects of Harvest of Nontimber Forest Products and Ecological Differences between Sites on the Demography of African Mahogany. Conservation Biology 24:605-614. doi:10.1111/j.1523-1739.2009.01345.x
study.notes: Six high-harvest vs six low-harvest populations (population-level mean matrices 2004-2006). Harvest status is not randomised: ecoregion and site differences are confounded.

study.citation: Gaoue OG, Horvitz CC, Ticktin T, Steiner UK, Tuljapurkar S (2013) Defoliation and bark harvesting affect life‐history traits of a tropical tree. Journal of Ecology 101:1563-1571. doi:10.1111/1365-2745.12140
study.notes: Same 12 populations re-censused 2004-2007. Intensity-class matrices (247640-247645) are pooled by ecoregion and intensity.

study.citation: Stewart KM (2001) The commercial bark harvest of the African cherry (Prunus africana) on Mount Oku, Cameroon (PhD thesis); matrices as archived in COMPADRE
study.site: Mount Oku, Cameroon (per thesis; COMPADRE plot labels only)
study.notes: One unharvested plot vs four harvested plots (once or twice per year), 1997-1999. No DOI; single control plot means the contrast has no replication on the control side. The thesis abstract reports lambda below 1 in harvested plots; 6 of 8 single-year harvested matrices here are below 1, but the 1997-99 mean matrices used for this comparison are at or above 1 in 3 of 4 plots. A later forest-wide harvest (2005/06) is outside these matrices (Stewart 2009, For Ecol Manage 258:1121).
study.citation_source: COMPADRE metadata (no DOI; thesis/grey literature, not independently verified)

study.citation: Hurlburt DP (1999) Population ecology and economic botany of Echinacea angustifolia, a native prairie medicinal plant (PhD/MSc thesis, Univ. of Kansas); matrices as archived in COMPADRE
study.notes: Harvested vs unmanipulated plants within two sites, 1996-1998. Thesis not peer-reviewed.
study.citation_source: COMPADRE metadata (no DOI; thesis/grey literature, not independently verified)

study.citation: Ticktin T, Ganesan R, Paramesha M, Setty S (2012) Disentangling the effects of multiple anthropogenic drivers on the decline of two tropical dry forest trees. Journal of Applied Ecology 49:774-784. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2664.2012.02156.x
study.site: Biligiri Rangaswamy Temple Wildlife Sanctuary, India
study.notes: Fruit-harvest matrices cover 1999-2006 whereas unmanipulated matrices cover 2006-2009: period and harvest are confounded. Mistletoe/Lantana co-drivers present. The authors conclude fruit harvest has little effect on stochastic growth and mistletoe drives decline; Prasad et al. 2014 (J Appl Ecol 51:642) dispute this, and the reply (51:648) attributes the post-ban rise to adult survival. The before/after contrast shown here is exactly the comparison in dispute.

study.citation: Groenendijk P, Eshete A, Sterck FJ, Zuidema PA, Bongers F (2012) Limitations to sustainable frankincense production: blocked regeneration, high adult mortality and declining populations. Journal of Applied Ecology 49:164-173. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2664.2011.02078.x
study.notes: Tapped vs untapped populations; the paper's conclusion is that both decline because of blocked regeneration (grazing, fire), independent of tapping.

study.citation: Pulido MT, Valverde T, Caballero J (2007) Variation in the population dynamics of the palm Sabal yapa in a landscape shaped by shifting cultivation in the Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico. Journal of Tropical Ecology 23:139-149. doi:10.1017/S0266467406003877
study.notes: Harvested palms are in crop fields; habitat and harvest fully confounded. Harvested organ is not the medicinal organ.

study.citation: Van der Voort ME, McGraw JB (2006) Effects of harvester behavior on population growth rate affects sustainability of ginseng trade. Biol Conserv 130:505-516
study.site: West Virginia, USA (COMPADRE gives no coordinates)

study.notes: Three harvester types simulated on field-measured West Virginia matrices (1998-2000): the treatments are model scenarios, not harvests observed in plots. Authors conclude state rules are not adequate to protect wild populations and that stewardship (later season, lower intensity, seed planting) can reverse decline.

study.citation: Winter S, Jung LS, Eckstein RL, Otte A, Donath TW, Kriechbaum M (2014) Control of the toxic plant Colchicum autumnale in semi-natural grasslands: effects of cutting treatments on demography and diversity. J Appl Ecol 51:524-533
study.product: none: cutting was applied to CONTROL a toxic plant, not to collect medicine
study.site: Six regions in Austria and Germany
study.notes: Randomised cutting plots, 2008-2011 mean matrices. COMPADRE labels the comparison plots 'Unmanipulated'; the paper describes them as cut in June (conventional management). The aim was to reduce a toxic weed, and the cut removes leaves, not the medicinal seeds or corms: use as evidence on the timing of leaf removal, not on medicinal collection.

study.notes: One Austrian flower-removal treatment against the June-cut plots (2008-2011 mean matrices). Single treatment and single region; weed-control purpose.

study.citation: Guedje NM, Zuidema PA, During H, Foahom B, Lejoly J (2007) Tree bark as a non-timber forest product [Garcinia lucida]. For Ecol Manage 240:1-12
study.product: bark and seeds (traded medicine, palm-wine additive)
study.site: Nyangong and Ebom, South Cameroon Atlantic forest
study.notes: Growth rate hides the damage here: the authors find the stock of harvestable trees falls to about half in 20 years under annual partial debarking and below 4% under annual ring-barking or felling, although lambda stays near 1. EthnoHarvest does not compute the harvestable stock. Matrix models for three local practices, built from a two-year field study (1997-1999); felling matrices have 9 stages, the others 8, so no LTRE is shown for felling.
